notes.summary: Matrices covers the order and types of matrices, equality, addition, scalar multiplication and multiplication, transpose, symmetric and skew-symmetric matrices, and the idea of an invertible matrix. CBSE tests it through 1-mark MCQs and assertion-reason items on orders, products, transposes and symmetric/skew-symmetric properties, plus short computations of products and unknown entries.
keyPoints: A matrix of order m × n has mn elements; a matrix with 12 elements can have orders 1×12, 12×1, 2×6, 6×2, 3×4 and 4×3 (one order for each divisor of 12).
Number of matrices of order m × n whose entries come from a set of k values = kᵐⁿ; e.g. 3 × 3 matrices with entries 0 or 1: 2⁹ = 512.
Equality: A = B only if both have the same order and every corresponding entry is equal — compare entry by entry to form equations.
The product AB exists only when columns of A = rows of B; (m × n)(n × p) gives m × p. In general AB ≠ BA, and AB = O does not force A = O or B = O.
Transpose rules: (Aᵀ)ᵀ = A, (kA)ᵀ = kAᵀ, (A + B)ᵀ = Aᵀ + Bᵀ, (AB)ᵀ = BᵀAᵀ (the order reverses).
Symmetric: Aᵀ = A (aᵢⱼ = aⱼᵢ). Skew-symmetric: Aᵀ = −A, so every diagonal entry is 0. For any square A: A + Aᵀ is symmetric, A − Aᵀ is skew-symmetric, and A = ½(A + Aᵀ) + ½(A − Aᵀ).
Invertible matrix: AB = BA = I; the inverse, if it exists, is unique and (AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹. An identity such as A² − 5A + 7I = O gives A⁻¹ = (5I − A)/7 after multiplying by A⁻¹.
Since A and I commute, the binomial expansion works for (I + A)ⁿ; it does not work for (A + B)² unless AB = BA, because (A + B)² = A² + AB + BA + B².
traps: Writing (A + B)² = A² + 2AB + B² or (A + B)(A − B) = A² − B² without checking that AB = BA.
Forgetting that the order reverses: writing (AB)ᵀ = AᵀBᵀ or (AB)⁻¹ = A⁻¹B⁻¹.
Mixing up aᵢⱼ: i is the row and j is the column, so a₂₃ is in row 2, column 3.
Assuming that if AB is defined then BA is defined and has the same order (2 × 3 times 3 × 2 gives 2 × 2, but the reverse product is 3 × 3).
Forgetting that the diagonal of a skew-symmetric matrix must be zero, while the diagonal of a symmetric matrix can be anything.
notes.examTip: Before multiplying, write the orders side by side as (m × n)(n × p) to check the product exists and find its order, then compute one entry at a time as row × column.

questions.text: For a 2 × 3 matrix A = [aᵢⱼ] whose elements are given by aᵢⱼ = 2i − j, the element a₂₃ is:
questions.explanation:
In aᵢⱼ, i is the row number and j is the column number.
For a₂₃: i = 2 and j = 3.
a₂₃ = 2(2) − 3 = 4 − 3 = 1.
(Using 2j − i by mistake gives 4.)

questions.text: The number of all possible matrices of order 3 × 3 with each entry 0 or 1 is:
questions.explanation:
A 3 × 3 matrix has 9 entries.
Each entry can be filled in 2 ways (0 or 1).
Total number of matrices = 2 × 2 × ... (9 times) = 2⁹ = 512.

questions.text:
Assertion (A): For any two square matrices A and B of the same order, AB = BA.
Reason (R): If A and B are square matrices of the same order, then both AB and BA are defined and have the same order.
Choose the correct option.
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true
questions.explanation:
R is true: for two n × n matrices, AB and BA are both defined and both are of order n × n.
A is false: being defined does not make them equal. For A = [[1, 0], [0, −1]] and B = [[0, 1], [1, 0]], AB = [[0, 1], [−1, 0]] but BA = [[0, −1], [1, 0]].
So A is false and R is true.

questions.text: If the matrix A = [[0, a, −3], [2, 0, −1], [b, 1, 0]] is skew-symmetric, then the values of a and b are:
questions.explanation:
For a skew-symmetric matrix, aᵢⱼ = −aⱼᵢ.
a₁₂ = −a₂₁ gives a = −2.
a₃₁ = −a₁₃ gives b = −(−3) = 3.
Check: a₂₃ = −1 and a₃₂ = 1, and all diagonal entries are 0, as required.
So a = −2 and b = 3.

questions.text: If A = [[3, 1], [−1, 2]] satisfies the equation A² − 5A + kI = O, where I is the 2 × 2 identity matrix and O is the zero matrix, then k equals:

A stationery shop sold pens and notebooks on two days. The quantity matrix (rows: Day 1, Day 2; columns: pens, notebooks) is Q = [[10, 5], [6, 8]], and the price matrix in rupees (rows: pen, notebook) is P = [[10], [40]]. Using the product QP, the total revenue of the shop over the two days is:
questions.explanation:
Q is 2 × 2 and P is 2 × 1, so QP is 2 × 1 and gives the revenue of each day.
Day 1: 10 × 10 + 5 × 40 = 100 + 200 = ₹300.
Day 2: 6 × 10 + 8 × 40 = 60 + 320 = ₹380.
Total revenue = 300 + 380 = ₹680. (Using QᵀP by mistake gives 340 + 370 = ₹710.)

questions.text: If A is a matrix of order 3 × 4 and B is a matrix such that both AᵀB and BAᵀ are defined, then the order of B is:
questions.explanation:
Aᵀ has order 4 × 3.
AᵀB is defined, so the number of rows of B = number of columns of Aᵀ = 3.
BAᵀ is defined, so the number of columns of B = number of rows of Aᵀ = 4.
Hence B is of order 3 × 4.

questions.text: Let R = [1  x  1] be a 1 × 3 row matrix, M = [[1, 3, 2], [2, 5, 1], [15, 3, 2]] and C = [[1], [2], [x]] a 3 × 1 column matrix. The values of x for which the product RMC = O are:
If A is a square matrix such that A² = A, then (I + A)³ − 7A equals:
questions.explanation:
Since A² = A, we get A³ = A²·A = A·A = A² = A.
I and A commute, so (I + A)³ = I + 3A + 3A² + A³.
= I + 3A + 3A + A = I + 7A.
Therefore (I + A)³ − 7A = I.
